dbf048cfbca0199e4255f28377908e66.text: The Williams Lake Fire Department responded to four dumpster fires in different areas of the city on Monday, Nov. 2. The City of Williams Lake is encouraging residents to remain vigilant after a series of dumpster fires broke out in a relatively short period of time. According to a Monday, Nov. 2 Facebook post the Williams Lake Fire Department responded to four small dumpster fires in different areas of the city over a period of approximately 45 minutes. “Crews responded quickly to each incident and were able to extinguish the fires before they spread,” the post read. “There were no injuries and no damage to surrounding property.” The city stated while there is currently no indication of a broader threat to public safety, residents are encouraged to remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity, smoke or fire concerns. Residents and businesses are also reminded to keep dumpsters clear of surrounding debris and combustible materials and, where possible, ensure dumpster lids and enclosures remain secured. “Thank you for looking out for one another and helping keep Williams Lake safe,” Mayor Surinderpal Rathor additionally wrote on Facebook.

c8a806c277fe7306695d904fc39baa28.text: A grizzly bear, like the one pictured here, is suspected to be behind the death of a hiker near Bella Coola. The BC Conservation Officer Service is investigating a suspected fatal bear attack near Bella Coola. The second victim of a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola has been located dead. The BC Conservation Officer Service said in a post on social media that the second victim was located this afternoon during search efforts by conservation officers and the RCMP. “Throughout the day, our priorities were to secure the area and protect officers and first responders as they searched for the missing person, then respectfully recover the deceased so they could be brought home to their family,” the post reads. “We extend our deepest condolences to both families. We remain committed to supporting them as our investigation continues.” BCCOS noted that officers continue to work to locate and capture any bears involved in the incident and added that it isn’t clear whether more than one bear was involved in the incident. The government agency said that any bears captured will be assessed to determine the appropriate next steps. If a bear is determined to be responsible for the attack, it will be dispatched to ensure public safety, in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines. “Search efforts have concluded. We continue to urge people to stay away from the Snooka West Trail area for their own safety and to give officers the space and time needed to do this work,” the post reads. BCCOS added they remain in regular contact with the Nuxalk Nation, members of the community and law enforcement as well as emergency response partners. The government agency added that further updates are expected as the investigation continues. One person has been found dead following a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, as search efforts continue for a second missing individual. 44620c28a5616a16f4e04111067e69bf.text: The Union of B.C. Municipalities had to appoint a new president following the Oct. 17 municipal elections. Following her unsuccessful mayoral bid, Squamish Coun. Jenna Stoner has been replaced as Union of B.C. Municipalities president just one month after taking the position. Per UBCM bylaws, first vice-president Sarrah Storey replaced Stoner. Incumbents fared poorly in municipal races across the province in the Oct. 17 local elections, and change on town and city councils also means change in umbrella organizations made up of local officials. “It’s a hard thing when we lose really great elected officials, and we lost a lot this year,” Storey said. Stoner was elected by acclamation in September at the UBCM conference in mid-September, and her term as president lasted only about one month. UBCM officials say they cannot find another instance of a president being forced out by losing a re-election bid. “I’m disappointed that I won’t be back around the table,” Stoner said. “The work that the organization does is very important and vital to all local government across the province. It was a real honour to be able to serve even a short term as president for that organization.” Stoner knew that running for mayor in Squamish risked her job as UBCM president, a role she was elevated to as a councillor. She ultimately lost the mayoral contest to Sean Easton by fewer than 200 votes. Six out of seven council seats in Squamish also turned over on Oct. 17, reflecting a wider provincewide trend of incumbents losing. Second vice-president Aimee Grice is out at UBCM as well, after losing her bid to move from council to the mayor’s office in Oliver. Despite the leadership changes, members set UBCM’s policy direction at a convention, and it should remain the same under Storey’s presidency. “My goal is to make sure that I am working on behalf of the priorities of our members, and those priorities obviously come from our resolutions and things that the members have identified,” Storey

Next summer’s FVDED in the Park dance music festival will grow to three days at Holland Park in Surrey. While no DJs are announced yet, the festival website shows 2027 dates of July 9, 10 and 11. FVDED has always been a two-day dance party in Surrey over the past decade-plus. “A 15-year milestone deserves main-character energy,” fest organizers post on social media Nov. 2. “FVDED is bringing 3 days, 4 stages and over 75+ international artists to Holland Park. Time to go big.” Festival “super early bird” tickets are sold on fvdedinthepark.com starting Tuesday, Nov. 10. Last July, an event-record 54,000 dance music fans showed up for the 2026 FVDED in the Park, featuring headliners Dom Dolla, Fisher, Griz and many others. Could the 2027 festival hit 80,000 attendance over three days? It’s possible. “We’ve been working for a couple years now to expand a bit,” festival founder/planner Alvaro Prol said last summer, hinting that “going three days in the future is the vision” for FVDED, co-produced by Blueprint Events and Live Nation Canada. “We’ve taken hits just like many others in recent years, with COVID, festivals going down, this and that, to be able to continue on,” Prol said in July. “Now the festival’s thriving, the future is really bright. 13ad3b5d3f70c340368dc6b5232d05ba.text: Joseph Camilleri, 76, completed the Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Challenge after crossing the finish line at the Berlin Marathon on Sept. 27. Victoria's Joseph Camilleri, known in the running community as "Crazy Legs," completed his sixth major marathon in Berlin, finishing the race in 4:51:25. Joseph Camilleri has run thousands of kilometres to reach the finish line. At 76, he finally has all six medals to show for it. The Victoria runner completed the Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Challenge on Sept. 27, crossing the finish line at the Berlin Marathon in 4:51:25 to complete a journey that began in Boston in 2018. The challenge requires runners to complete six of the world’s major marathons: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York City. Born in Malta, Camilleri first moved to England, then came to Canada in 1972 at 22 years old, joining his brother in Winnipeg. He later moved to Toronto before landing in Victoria in 2010. He said his research suggests he is the oldest Maltese-Canadian athlete to complete the challenge, a distinction that makes the accomplishment even more special. Known around Victoria’s running community as “Crazy Legs,” Camilleri’s final marathon came after a difficult year of injuries, setbacks and uncertainty about whether he would make it to the starting line. In conversation with Black Press Media, Camilleri said he began training specifically for Berlin in May, but suffered a slipped disc in June that left him unable to exercise, even on a stationary bike. After physiotherapy and chiropractic treatment, the pain eventually subsided in early August. He returned to running, only to fall twice within a matter of weeks, further aggravating an ongoing knee injury. The problems continued overseas. Ten days before the Berlin Marathon, while visiting Malta, Camilleri couldn’t complete a four-kilometre run. A sports doctor administered an injection and advised him not to run for 10 days. 71f6c78a417878011949341b261d8516.text: A growing memorial for the victims in the Lapu Lapu Day festival attack sits at the corner of East 41st Avenue and Fraser Street. Friday, May 2 was a provincial day of mournlng and remembrance for the attack that killed 11 and injured at least two dozen others on April 26, 2025. Adam Kai-Ji Lo, the accused in the fatal car ramming at the 2025 Lapu Lapu event in Vancouver, has pleaded not guilty to all charges. The B.C. Prosecution Service confirmed to Today In BC that Lo pleaded not guilty to the 11 second-degree murder charges and the additional 31 attempted murder charges in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver on Monday (Nov. 2). Lo is in the midst of a 22-day voir dire, a mini hearing to determine whether evidence can be admitted at trial. A provincial court judge, Reginald Harris, found him mentally fit to stand trial on Sept. 10, 2025. The trial was moved to B.C. Supreme Court earlier this year. He is expected to stand trial beginning April 19, 2027, at the Vancouver Law Courts. The trial is expected to continue for four months. The B.C. Prosecution Service says pretrial applications are currently underway and are expected to continue until mid-March 2027. Lo is accused of driving an SUV into a crowd of people at the Lapu Lapu Day block party in Vancouver on April 26, 2025. He was arrested at the scene. Eleven people were killed – seven women, two men, one non-binary person and a five-year-old girl – and at least two dozen more were injured, ranging in age from 22 months old to 60 years old. Initially charged with eight counts of second-degree murder the day after the incident, another three second-degree murder charges were approved by the prosecution service on July 22, 2025. He was then charged with 31 counts of attempted murder after he was found fit to stand trial. **News** **Union of B.C. Municipalities appoints new president after incumbent loses mayoral

6368de38b45ff9703f80b7edf3b643b0.text: **Friday, Oct. 30 – Quesnel River Rush 2, Fernie Ghostriders 10** The Quesnel River Rush struggled to contain the Fernie Ghostriders, falling 10-2 Friday night at the West Fraser Centre. Fernie wasted little time getting on the scoreboard, striking four times in the opening period to take a commanding 4-0 lead. Sawyer Samycia opened the scoring just 54 seconds into the game, followed by goals from Liam Breakenridge at 4:40, Carter Singleton at 9:09 and Ethan Watkins at 10:34. The Ghosriders continued their offensive push in the second period, adding more goals to extend their advantage to 8-0. Breakenridge added his second goal of the night at 12:18, converting on the power play to restore Fernie’s nine-goal advantage and seal the 10-2 final. Quesnel RCMP are warning the public against taking the law into their own hands after a stolen vehicle was involved in a serious collision Sunday afternoon. According to an RCMP press release, a brown Ford F-250 was reported stolen from a property on Pentland Crescent during the early morning hours of Oct. 30. Mounties said on Nov. 1 that a member of the public spotted the vehicle near the Kersley General Store. A second witness spotted the vehicle near Highway 97 and Racing Road and pursued it at high speeds into downtown Quesnel. Shortly before 3 p.m., the truck collided with an uninvolved Ford Focus at the intersection of Kinchant Street and Carson Avenue. Although no serious injuries were reported, RCMP said the incident highlights the dangers of members of the public attempting to intervene in criminal matters themselves. “We are reminding the public of the dangers of taking the law into your own hands; thankfully, there were no serious injuries in this collision, but that doesn’t justify the actions of anyone involved,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said. “As a member of the public, there is no way for you to know any previous police or criminal history of the person you are dealing with and the dangers you are exposing yourself or those around you to.” Mounties have identified a man they believe was driving the stolen vehicle and are searching for him after he left the collision scene. According to the release, the individual is known to police. The recovered truck has been seized and towed to a secure location as the investigation continues. Quesnel RCMP are asking anyone who witnessed the incident and has not yet spoken with investigators to come forward. 1555fb10b5d9ab3c82932f1ed034254d.text: Award-winning documentary on 2018 northern B.C. wildfires coming to Williams Lake | Williams Lake Tribune Award-winning documentary on 2018 northern B.C. wildfires coming to Williams Lake The Fire In Our Hearts, an award-winning wildfire documentary, is coming to Williams Lake on Nov. 7 and Nov. 12 at Paradise CInemas. As wildfires raged in 2018 forcing his friends, family and neighbours to choose to evacuate or remain to protect the land that defines them filmmaker Josias Tschanz knew he wanted to give his remote community in northern B.C. a voice. Tschanz is bringing his feature length award-winning documentary that he hopes will spark discussion, The Fire In Our Hearts, to Williams Lake on Saturday, Nov. 7 and Thursday, Nov. 12. The film follows communities located directly south of Francois Lake and tells the story of ordinary residents, First Nations and firefighters who chose flight over flight.. “At first it was not a film,” Tschanz said noting, he immigrated to Canada when he was 16 years old from Switzerland and his parents live in the area. At the time of the fires that resulted in ferry access being restricted, Tschanz was smuggled through the toxic smoke on a shipping boat with a friend. “It was just to document things and then create a GoFundMe page, and we had a video that would help people that had lost a lot in the community, but then what happened was the beautiful story of the community coming together and forming an organization.” That organization, Tschanz, said is the Chinook Emergency Response Society which is now a national blueprint on how smaller communities can be part of the solution when there is wildfire and they are too remote to access and provide resources and time. This is where the story takes off, according to Tschanz, telling more than just the fires themselves but the aftermath and what happened during that time. 945d236cc2dcdb75cc057681ec165d65.text: A white shuttle bus that crashed in the ditch off Highway 39 near MacKenzie on Nov. 4, 2026. B.C. Highway Patrol is looking for witnesses and video footage of a bus crash that left 20 people injured. Police received a call about a single-vehicle crash on Highway 39, about four kilometres south of Mackenzie, on Wednesday at 9:10 a.m., according to an updated release from B.C. Highway Patrol Wednesday afternoon. When officers arrived, they found a northbound white shuttle bus in a ditch. There were about 20 passengers and the driver with injuries ranging from minor to serious, police said. “This was a chaotic scene, and police will need time to sort out many of the details,” B.C. Highway Patrol Sgt. Michael McLaughlin said. Multiple air and ground ambulances were called in to get those injured treatment. There was also a complete shutdown of the portion of Highway 39. RCMP collision analysts were also called in. Police say no arrests have been made, but the cause of the crash is uncertain. McLaughlin said police are now looking to speak to anyone who has dash-camera video of the bus, or any witnesses who say what happened prior to the crash. If anyone saw the bus in the minutes before the collision, or you have video footage, they’re asked to call B.C. Highway Patrol – Prince George at 250-649-4004 and quote file (3100) 2026-956.

ee78d4bec377f01f29c1eb0cadf45249.text: B.C.’s Civil Resolution Tribunal declined to charge the social media platform X an additional $100,000 penalty for failing to remove intimate images from its platform. Instead of taking down the images entirely, X “geoblocked” them so they cannot be viewed legally in Canada. While this fails to adhere to the letter of the law, the company successfully argued that the tribunal could not enforce B.C. law outside Canada, and that X had made a reasonable attempt to comply. The B.C. legislature passed the Intimate Images Protection Act in 2023. It was created to give people a way to stop non-consensual intimate images of themselves from being shared online. In March 2025, the Civil Resolution Tribunal granted a request from an unnamed applicant and ordered X to take down some images. X tried to argue that the posts did not qualify as “intimate images” under this law. The tribunal disagreed, fining the company $100,000 and ordering it to remove the images. When the images were geoblocked instead of deleted, the plaintiff filed an application for another order and another fine. Tribunal vice-chair Eric Regehr found that “geoblocking” to prevent an image being shown in a particular area is not the same as deleting an image and therefore doesn’t really comply with the strict terms of the takedown order. But Regehr also acknowledges companies must have some leeway. Before the law passed, then-Attorney General Niki Sharma told a legislative committee that the intention was “if you take reasonable actions, your liability is limited.” The company also contends that B.C. can’t force it, as an American company, to obey the province’s laws in the U.S. X brought in an expert to testify that the images wouldn’t violate U.S. law, which is far more protective of freedom of speech than Canadian law. “X argues that it would be unreasonable to expect it to strictly comply with B.C. law by deleting the image, with global effect, when United States law would not require it to remove the

a7ed4d23127bc9e862ec532116de1bb0.text: U.S. skiers latest to be fined for entering closed backcountry in Rogers Pass | Williams Lake Tribune U.S. skiers latest to be fined for entering closed backcountry in Rogers Pass Views from Loop Brook Trail in Glacier National Park pictured Feb. 17, 2025. Two U.S. skiers are the latest to be penalized by a provincial court judge for entering a backcountry area of Rogers Pass that was closed for avalanche risk. Jacob A. Gordon and Jack William Elder appeared at the Revelstoke Courthouse on Oct. 7, each charged on one count of prohibited or restricted activity under Section 7.4 of Parks Canada’s general regulations. On April 14, the two men parked their Montana plate-bearing vehicle at the Loop Brook parking lot in Glacier National Park to go ski touring. They set off into the West Rogers Winter Restricted Area, which, unbeknownst to them, Parks Canada had closed earlier that day due to avalanche conditions and potential need for howitzer-based avalanche control. The pair of experienced skiers had avalanche training and familiarity with Rogers Pass and the Canadian Rockies, and arrived that day with valid 2025-26 winter permits. They’d checked Avalanche Canada’s bulletin for advisories in the park. However, the men failed to consult Parks Canada’s online map that’s updated every morning to show which areas in Glacier are closed. Entering Loop Brook, they would’ve passed signage reminding them to check that map. Parks Canada avalanche officer Ross Campbell later noticed a vehicle, registered under Gordon’s name, and reported it being there illegally, as the parking lot was closed along with the West Rogers area. A park warden responded, contacting Gordon by phone to direct him and Elder to return to the parking lot immediately. They reappeared within two hours of first departing for the Loop Brook backcountry, and “were remorseful and polite,” federal prosecutor Lucille Bordeleau told Justice George Leven in Revelstoke. 294288601664170912cb8e3e9a6ca8e9.text: NDP House Leader Mike Farnworth hopes the U.S. midterm results begin to mend neighbourly relations with Canada. Some B.C. politicians were optimistic that the Democrats’ sweeping midterm gains could help ease trade tensions with the United States, but incoming premier Lorne Doerkson expressed doubt. He is skeptical that the midterm results would suddenly end the trade war and allow goods to flow freely between the countries again. “I don’t see that happening next week, and I wish it would,” he said. Doerkson called Trump a “bully” and blamed the NDP government for failing to ready the province’s industry for this threat. He says that if the “frustration” of the trade war continues, he will not rescind the ban on U.S. alcohol products in BC Liquor stores. “With respect to any conversations going forward, I am all ears and obviously want to work with anybody who wants to support and build British Columbia,” he said. Those on the left side of the political spectrum were far more effervescent than those on the right as they relished the moment. “I think it was a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump and everything he’s tried to do to the United States and to Canada, and I am absolutely thrilled,” B.C. NDP House Leader Mike Farnworth said. “He is absolutely the worst president that country has ever had.” Farnworth hopes the result leads to a return to “sanity” in trade negotiations, though he acknowledges this won’t be easy as each side continues to pursue its own best interests. “One hopes that it leads to a recognition by the U.S. that we are their neighbour,” he said. “We have been their best friend, and it would be nice to see us being treated in a way that is not detrimental, like we have seen under Trump.” Interim NDP Leader Jennifer Whiteside says the results prove the trade war hurts people on both sides of the border, and the Democrats’ victory “better positions” Canadians seeking a deal. A man with Victoria connections, who bludgeoned his new wife Iris McNeil to death in their Lower Mainland home while she slept in the summer of 1997 has once again been denied parole. The Parole Board of Canada denied both parole and day parole for James Shortreed, who beat McNeil with a claw hammer and stabbed her with a knife then stuffed her body into a freezer on July 23, 1997. The now 71-year-old would “present an undue risk to society if released,” the decision reads. “Regarding conditional release, you acknowledge that you are not ready for full parole. On day parole, you wish to be released to Vancouver Island, which is your preferred release destination. However, consultations with Community-Based Residential Facilities (CBRFs) in that area resulted in your request for residency being declined. The facilities advised that you require a further period of sustained stability at minimum security and additional development of your release plans before they would consider accepting you.” Shortreed indicated connections to AA members in Victoria who would support him — all served or are currently serving as escorts at the minimum-security facility where he’s incarcerated. His only family members live in another province. Sentenced to life for second-degree murder in 1999, Shortreed already had a violent criminal history including his first federal sentence in 1991 for two counts of sexual assault with a weapon and forcible confinement against his common-law spouse. He also had a 1974 conviction for attempted rape. He was denied parole and unescorted temporary absences in October 2021. Between 2010 and 2019, he was approved for unescorted temporary absences for personal development and community service. Those were were stopped due to COVID in early 2020. 37bc83222d00ff24088fbe5a975a1c46.text: Joseph Camilleri, 76, completed the Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Challenge after crossing the finish line at the Berlin Marathon on Sept. 27. Victoria's Joseph Camilleri, known in the running community as "Crazy Legs," completed his sixth major marathon in Berlin, finishing the race in 4:51:25. Joseph Camilleri has run thousands of kilometres to reach the finish line. At 76, he finally has all six medals to show for it. The Victoria runner completed the Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Challenge on Sept. 27, crossing the finish line at the Berlin Marathon in 4:51:25 to complete a journey that began in Boston in 2018. The challenge requires runners to complete six of the world’s major marathons: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York City. Born in Malta, Camilleri first moved to England, then came to Canada in 1972 at 22 years old, joining his brother in Winnipeg. He later moved to Toronto before landing in Victoria in 2010. He said his research suggests he is the oldest Maltese-Canadian athlete to complete the challenge, a distinction that makes the accomplishment even more special. Known around Victoria’s running community as “Crazy Legs,” Camilleri’s final marathon came after a difficult year of injuries, setbacks and uncertainty about whether he would make it to the starting line. In conversation with Black Press Media, Camilleri said he began training specifically for Berlin in May, but suffered a slipped disc in June that left him unable to exercise, even on a stationary bike. After physiotherapy and chiropractic treatment, the pain eventually subsided in early August. He returned to running, only to fall twice within a matter of weeks, further aggravating an ongoing knee injury. The problems continued overseas. Ten days before the Berlin Marathon, while visiting Malta, Camilleri couldn’t complete a four-kilometre run. A sports doctor administered an injection and advised him not to run for 10 days. The Tŝideldel Post Office opened Nov. 2 at 710 Redstone Flats, following years of work by Tŝideldel Development Corporation and Canada Post to bring postal services into the community. Clayton Charleyboy, an elected Tŝideldel First Nation councillor and the executive director of Tŝideldel Development Corporation, said residents expressed pride that their mailing addresses will now identify their community rather than neighbouring Chilanko Forks. “So our identity was tied to somewhere we didn’t live,” he said. “We are in the Chilcotin, far away from major cities. We have been displaced a few times, and Tŝideldel is the last place we ended up, so Tŝideldel means home to me,” said Otis Guichon Sr., Nits’ilʔin (Chief) of Tŝideldel First Nation in the media release by Tŝideldel Development Corporation and Canada Post Beyond the name on the address, Charleyboy said the outlet gives residents access to mail in a secure, lit and maintained setting within their community. 59ca811dc5854047bba7ecb8aee38eda.text: Environment Canada is warning on Nov. 5, 2026 of moderate to strong gusty winds in the southern Interior. A special weather statement is warning of moderate to strong gusty winds for several regions in the Interior. According to the statement by Environment Canada on Thursday, Nov. 5, the winds are expected to start Thursday evening and last until Friday evening in the Cariboo, Prince George, 100 Mile House (including Highway 97) and South Thompson regions. The weather alert states it is for the south Cariboo including Williams Lake. “A strong low pressure system will approach the B.C. coast this evening and will bring a prolonged period of southeast winds with gusts ranging from 60-70 km/h to the B.C. interior,” the statement says. The southeast winds will pick up in the evening and are expected to peak by Friday morning. They may ease slightly on Friday afternoon before an incoming cold front is expected to bring a strong push of southwest winds, with gusts possibly up to 90 km/h between Quesnel and Prince George. Winds for the South Thompson region are expected to peak Friday afternoon, with the strongest winds expected near Cache Creek. A potentially stronger storm is set to follow on Saturday evening, Environment Canada says. “Local utility outages are possible. Parks and forests may sustain damage. Secure loose objects,” the statement reads. “Weather in the mountains can change suddenly resulting in hazardous driving conditions.” “Please continue to monitor alerts and forecasts issued by Environment Canada. To report severe weather, send an email to BCstorm@ec.gc.ca or post reports on social media using #BCStorm.”

a5c2f2a0d25f5420a0f14b0396f04d1e.text: The 2026 federal budget includes $6.5 billion to support the forestry industry. Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne unveiled the 2026 budget in Ottawa on Thursday, promising a slew of initiatives to help boost the economy amid trade uncertainty. Titled “Masters of Our Destiny,” the budget document is fully geared toward protecting Canadian economic sovereignty. It also keeps spending in the red for the foreseeable future. This budget projects a $62.3-billion deficit this fiscal year, which would grow slightly to $62.5 billion next year, then fall to $57.6 billion the year after. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre took to social media, calling it a “credit card budget” and saying it will cause Canada’s debt to soar and mean “higher taxes tomorrow.” The forestry sector is set to gain, with $6.5 billion earmarked for the industry over the next six years. This adds to the $2.9 billion announced to support forestry since August 2025. According to the budget, the new funding is to be spent on increasing fibre supply, modernizing forestry facilities, supporting higher-value product production and expanding market opportunities. Most of this money, $4 billion, is slated for a new Forestry Sector Accelerator to invest in large biorefineries, biofuel facilities and other “higher-value” forestry production. Kim Haakstad, president of the B.C. Council of Forest Industries, welcomed the finding, but said funding alone won’t save the sector. “We need a clear strategy with concrete actions and timelines to get more wood moving, attract investment and protect forestry jobs and communities,” she said in a written statement. The budget also seeks to boost support for western resource extraction by offering to sell a 15-per-cent stake in the Trans Mountain Corporation, owner of the TMX oil pipeline, to 128 individual Indigenous groups in B.C. and Alberta. Members of the white nationalist group Loyalist Pioneers were seen on the steps of the B.C. Legislature on Oct. 25, the morning following the 2026 provincial election. Victoria resident Julie Baetz was on her daily commute to work when she spotted a peculiar sight at the B.C. Legislature. A dozen people, all dressed in black and wearing masks, walked up the steps of the legislative building before unfurling a banner bearing the word “remigration” and the name Loyalist Pioneers. Watching from a distance, Baetz took a few pictures, and a quick online search confirmed her suspicion that the group was a white nationalist organization, making an appearance the day following the Oct. 24 provincial election, in which Conservatives won a sweeping majority. According to the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, the group is classified as part of the “white nationalism 3.0” or “Active Club” movement — an emerging decentralized network of alt-right groups using physical fitness, combat sports, and camaraderie to recruit members into white supremacist and extremist activities. Spreading across Canada over the past few years, the group is part of a broader movement that includes Second Sons and Nationalist-13, whose primary focus is anti-immigration. The word “remigration,” displayed on the group’s banner, is a modern political buzzword used by far-right movements to promote the mass deportation or forced expulsion of immigrants and their descendants. b2ac268cb152c6a4ae288c92468863ce.text: Panago was first started in Abbotsford in 1986, growing to 170 locations by 2026. Panago's head office is located in Abbotsford, which is where the pizza chain first started in 1986. What started as a small group of Abbotsford pizzerias in 1986 has since grown to approximately 170 locations all across Canada. Panago was first launched under the name Panagopoulos 2 for 1 Pizza Place by the Rooke family, who also created several other local businesses. After a number of name changes and expansions in the decade after opening, the company also added Sean DeGregorio to its team, who now serves as Panago’s CEO. Being involved from so early on in the company’s journey has been a special experience, said DeGregorio. He’s also particularly proud that what started as an Abbotsford company, and is still headquartered in the city, has been able to achieve such growth in just 40 years. “It was the people of Abbotsford who gave us a chance and kept coming back for pizza,” said DeGregorio. “We owe this community a lot.” Panago now employs nearly 3,000 people across its 170 locations, and sells more than six million pizzas per year. “I’m proud of our local owners and their teams,” said DeGregorio. “They’re the ones making the pizza and giving people a reason to come back, just like they did here.” As part of the pizza chain’s 40th birthday celebration, Panago has launched special promotions throughout November. Many locations will also host a Customer Appreciation Day event on Nov. 29 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. “Our 40th birthday is an opportunity to thank the customers, franchisees, and communities who have been part of Panago’s journey,” said DeGregorio. “We’re proud of how far we’ve come and excited to celebrate this milestone with the people who helped make it possible.”

Four Canadian Armed Forces members injured in the fire at CFB Wainwright have been transferred to health-care facilities in B.C. and Ontario. The transfers follow “careful medical assessment and recommendations from medical professionals,” according to the latest update from the Department of National Defence Wednesday (Nov. 4). The four were moved to be closer to their home communities where they can continue receiving the medical care they need, while being closer to family and loved ones, the update adds. Twenty-five people remain hospitalized, while 14 others have since been released from hospital. Four soldiers, Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, were killed. “Recovery will look different for each injured person and their family. Some may face a long journey ahead, but they will not face it alone,” the statement says. The Military Police has been tasked with an independent investigation into the fire. It’s being conducted independently of the Canadian Armed Forces chain of command, an Oct. 22 update said. A Board of Inquiry will also be conducted as a separate and independent process. The department says those are typically conducted following the completion of an investigation, but they could happen concurrently when doing so does not compromise the integrity of the investigative processes. The department says the boards of inquiry are led by the Canadian Armed Forces and they are fact-finding investigations “which will try to determine how an incident came about and whether any lessons can be learned from it to prevent recurrence.” On Oct. 17, a fire was reported on an automatic grenade launcher range which initiated during routine military training activities, according to an Oct. 22 statement from the Canadian Forces provost marshal. 41903273abf5b2735e0aa8ea7a65025f.text: Elections BC is set to begin finalizing the vote for the 2026 previncial election. Elections BC says it is set to begin counting roughly 150,000 absentee, mail-in and assisted telephone ballots not included in initial election-day counts. This will add significantly to the nearly 1.8 million ballots counted so far in the 2026 provincial election and could alter the result in several races. In Cowichan Valley, Conservative Bert Chen leads NDP’s Debra Toporowski by 151 votes. In Kelowna Centre, Conservative Kristina Loewen is ahead of the NDP’s Loyal Wooldridge by 132 votes. In Burnaby South-Metrotown, the NDP’s Paul Choi leads Conservative David Xie by 66 votes. NDP candidate Stephanie Higginson holds a razor-thin lead in Ladysmith-Oceanside. She leads Conservative Kris McNichol by just 13 votes. Those last two ridings are undergoing recounts, which are triggered when the margin is fewer than 100 votes. Five additional ridings have current margins of fewer than 500 votes, and seven more have margins of fewer than 1,000. Counting for the new batch of ballots will begin Friday, Nov. 6, and is expected to be completed on Nov. 10, when Elections BC will finalize results. These new ballots are sealed in certification envelopes to be checked before opening against votes cast on election day to prevent double voting. This marks the official end of vote-counting. The writs are to be returned on Nov. 18, allowing for members of the legislature to be sworn in. Conservative MLAs are scheduled to be sworn in on Nov. 19, Green Party MLAs on Nov. 23 and NDP MLAs on Nov. 26. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has not yet said whether the legislature will hold a short fall session.

A sample of some of the names, phrases and slogans written, inked or carved into the bridge in Centennial Park. One defining part of being human is wanting to be remembered. While that’s not quite universal, as plenty of people are content to go about their lives quietly, I would argue we all, on some level, want to be remembered by our friends and loved ones. We want to leave our mark on the world while we are here and after we, inevitably, are gone. I got to thinking about this recently while walking through Centennial Park, specifically across the bridge by Bridge Creek Falls. Along the wooden railings, you will often find graffiti, carved names and messages. Now, you might be inclined to dismiss such markings as vandalism and move on, but I stopped to think about the reasoning behind the messages written in pencil, marker or with the tip of a knife. On the one hand, it’s the action of bored individuals, but on the other, it is the continuation of a tradition as old as humanity. For millennia, we have sought to leave our mark on things that will outlast us. During the Stone Age, our ancestors would paint or carve scenes of everyday life into caves that either served as their homes or ritual spaces. Who these early artists were is long lost to us, yet their work remains. As agriculture was adopted and the first civilizations formed, this impulse to record our lives carried on. Egyptian Pharaohs recorded on their monuments and tombs the stories of their lives and those of their people.
